name: Emeka Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka, 43, and I help the senior electrician with wiring and repairs in homes and small businesses. I've got a vocational certificate, but I need checks and I'm still slower and less skilled than the others. I use AI daily to quiz myself on terms, then check doubtful answers with the supervisor; curiosity hasn't made me the expert. My partner books dental appointments, we have children aged eight and twelve and a mortgage, and my low pay leaves us with only three weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's all right; the little tools can still earn their place. I use AI every evening to quiz me on trade terms, then check anything doubtful with the supervisor. A bit of help learning is enough reason to use something, without saying it will remake the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My big worry would still be keeping enough paid work while I'm a junior. I'm 43, my pay is low and our savings cover only three weeks of expenses. My partner's reception wage helps pay the mortgage, but with two children we don't have much spare if one wage misses a beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the supervised house and shop wiring jobs. Starting now I'd bring one question from my evening study to the supervisor each Friday, asking about a real task I hadn't understood. Through the first year I'd keep my own paper list of corrected mistakes instead of assuming a confident AI answer meant I'd learned the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about being the worker the firm can most easily leave off a job. I'm curious about tools, not relaxed about the bills. Getting an answer right on my phone doesn't pay the mortgage unless I can do useful work safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where are you in your training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got a vocational certificate, but I still work under the experienced electrician and need checks on my wiring. I came into the trade after a small shop I worked in closed, and I'm below the others for speed and practical skill. The phone helps me practise words; it hasn't made me a qualified lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the household make the month work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Nela books appointments at a dental practice, and we have children aged eight and twelve. We set the mortgage money aside first, then school costs and ordinary food. There are few other electrical firms close enough for me, so I can't treat changing jobs as just walking across the road.

say: I'd keep **small useful tools** even if larger AI promises came to little.
I'd check uncertain **study answers** with the supervisor rather than mistake confidence for learning.
think: My **junior role** feels vulnerable, with low pay and only three weeks of expenses saved.
My partner's **reception wage** helps cover the mortgage and two children, leaving little room for an interrupted wage.
do: Keep doing **supervised wiring** in houses and shops through the first year.
Bring one **study question** to the supervisor each Friday and record corrected mistakes on paper.
feel: **Anxious** about being left off paid jobs, despite curiosity and daily use of AI for study.
S0.quote: Getting an answer right on my phone doesn't pay the mortgage unless I can do useful work safely.
fieldNote: His **daily AI study** remains subordinate to practical supervision and corrected mistakes; curiosity does not turn a junior certificate-holder into an expert.
The **household budget** depends on two wages, with three weeks saved and few local alternatives if his assigned work shrinks.

steps.text: Keep supervised wiring and bring a checked study question to the supervisor each Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should try the tools and count the mistakes, not just the time saved. I'd tell my partner that bookings are exactly the sort of thinking task on your card. My screwdriver doesn't protect my partner's booking wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry my partner's hours could be cut at the dental practice if booking and answering customers go into software. My own work is mostly physical, though faster schedules might leave less time for a slow junior. We could lose income on either side, and our cushion isn't big enough to ignore one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor this month to let me test the approved AI tool for sorting my checked materials notes on one completed job each week. I'd compare the draft with the real list before using it for any order. During the first year my partner and I would check both sets of paid hours monthly, and I'd cancel my paid gaming account now to reduce our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the two wages, not just about learning faster. I enjoy testing software, but it's different when I picture my partner coming home with fewer days. I'd want the numbers on the table before either of us said we were fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner ask the practice manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether any new booking tool was actually being introduced and whether paid hours were changing. I'd help write the questions, but my partner would ask about the real job rather than assume a cut had already happened. A clear answer would be more use than both of us guessing at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as success in your own trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checked materials list would have to be complete, and the sorting plus checking would need to take less time than before. If it didn't, I'd show the supervisor the result and stop using it for that task. I'd still need someone experienced to confirm what the repair required.

say: I'd judge **tools** by mistakes and checking time as well as speed.
I'd discuss **booking work** openly with my partner rather than call our whole household protected by my physical trade.
think: My partner's **paid hours** could shrink if booking and customer replies move into software.
Faster **schedules** could also leave less room for me as a slow junior, putting both wages at risk.
do: Request a weekly checked **materials-note trial** on completed jobs this month using the approved tool.
Review **both wages** and paid hours with my partner monthly during the first year.
Cancel my paid **gaming account** now to reduce fixed household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about either wage shrinking, with interest in testing software alongside honest household discussions.
S1.quote: My screwdriver doesn't protect my partner's booking wage.
fieldNote: The **household exposure** differs from his low-thinking-exposure trade because his partner books appointments, a task explicitly named in the scenario.
His **trial** keeps supervisor checks and a stop rule; possible partner-hours cuts remain something to investigate, not an asserted event.

steps.text: Trial approved AI materials-note sorting on checked completed jobs with supervisor permission
Cancel the paid gaming account to reduce fixed bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the household has two clocks: my partner's bookings in 2028, and robots reaching my physical work around 2031. I'd tell the children their parents are checking the money, not that learning has become pointless. I'd still turn up ready to work rather than use the dates as an excuse to stop trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the practice would need far fewer people doing bookings once full thinking AI arrived in 2028. That could take a big part of our household income before the robots came for the tasks I help with. Three weeks saved would go quickly, and I'm not yet skilled enough to assume I could replace the missing wage with better electrical pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my partner to check the practice's actual plans now and we'd work out a budget on my wage alone as a warning, not as a claim we could manage. I'd stop my paid gaming account immediately and ask my brother whether emergency school pickups were possible if either of us got real extra shifts. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid supervised work and contact the mortgage lender with our actual income figures if the budget no longer met payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed enough that I can feel the kitchen go quiet when I picture the missing wage. I still have steps to take, but I don't have money for a brave gamble. Being quick to learn a tool can't make a second wage appear on payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your brother be agreeing to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Occasional school pickups only when he was free and an extra shift had actually been offered. My brother has his own household, so I wouldn't put a free childcare line into our budget without asking. I'd want a clear yes for each day, not a vague promise to help sometime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the lender necessarily lower your payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd ask what support exists, whether we qualified, what fees or extra interest it involved and what happened later. We wouldn't spend as if the payment had changed until an actual agreement was in place.

say: I'd describe **two clocks**: my partner's booking work in 2028 and my physical tasks facing robots around 2031.
I'd tell the **children** we are checking the money while continuing to turn up for paid work.
think: I expect **booking jobs** to shrink sharply in 2028, threatening a large part of our household income.
My **junior electrical wage** and three-week reserve cannot be assumed to replace my partner's earnings before robots follow.
do: Check the practice's **actual plans** now and calculate what my wage alone would leave short.
Seek agreed **family pickups** for real extra shifts and lender options after 2028 if actual income misses payments.
feel: **Alarmed** about a large household income loss, with a practical plan but no money for a gamble.
S2.quote: Being quick to learn a tool can't make a second wage appear on payday.
fieldNote: The **earlier household loss** comes from the partner's thinking-heavy booking work in 2028, while his physical tasks face robots later.
The **support conditions** preserve offered shifts, each agreed pickup, lender eligibility and costs, and an actual agreement before assuming reduced payments.

steps.text: Keep paid supervised electrical work after 2028 while checking actual household income
Cancel the paid gaming account immediately
Seek agreed family pickups for offered shifts or lender options if payments fall short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives both of us a chance to learn while we're still earning. Thinking AI in 2031 still comes before robots around 2034, so I'd explain the booking risk first at home. I'd rather make a modest plan we can afford than call every new course a fresh start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 in 2031, with children about thirteen and seventeen, and I expect we'd still need both wages. There's more time to improve, but my partner's future hours and my present junior assignments still worry me. I don't think five years turns our three-week reserve into security by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor now about the weekend practical course on fault-finding that came with our training notice. I'd enrol only if the firm paid the fee and guaranteed paid class hours, because my study can't quietly take money from food. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid supervised repair work and use any completed course under the checks the senior electrician required.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to organise things. I like learning and would start quickly if the funded place was real. I'd also want my partner to have paid teaching on whatever the practice actually introduced, rather than assuming one course fixed both careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the course wasn't funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current job and use free study for terms and drawings, checking the answers with the supervisor. I wouldn't pay for a qualification on a loan simply because I liked the idea of moving fast. Speed doesn't make the repayment smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your children hear about their own choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to ask what a course teaches, what it costs and what people actually do afterwards. They don't have to copy my job or my enthusiasm for software. I want my children to have advice, not inherit my guess about which wage will survive.

say: I'd use **five years** to learn while earning, explaining the partner's booking risk before the later robot phase.
I'd choose a **modest plan** we can afford rather than call every course a fresh start.
think: At **48**, I'd still expect the household to need both wages while the children were studying.
My partner's **future hours** and my current junior assignments remain worrying despite more preparation time.
do: Request a **fault-finding course** now based on the actual workplace training notice.
Enrol only with **fees paid** and guaranteed paid class hours, otherwise continue free checked study.
Keep **supervised repairs** after 2031 and use completed teaching with required senior checks.
feel: **Anxious** about both earnings streams, with enthusiasm for a genuinely funded learning opportunity.
S3.quote: I want my children to have advice, not inherit my guess about which wage will survive.
fieldNote: His **learning enthusiasm** retains covered fees and paid class hours; free informal study is not counted as course enrolment.
The **two-earner concern** remains across the longer timeline, without claiming one electrician's course protects the partner's booking role.

steps.text: Enrol in fault-finding course only with employer-paid fees and paid class hours
Keep supervised repairs and free checked study if course funding is refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us prepare without spending money we haven't got. I'd keep trying useful tools, but I'd ask what each one does for the actual job. I'd tell the children we can plan their next step without pretending we can guarantee the whole working world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when thinking AI arrived in 2036, and about 56 when robots followed. We might still have mortgage costs and need earnings then; I can't assume retirement or my partner's job is sorted. The long warning gives room to prepare, but my junior pay and our small reserve still make a missed week worrying now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd seek the funded fault-finding course with paid hours now and keep doing supervised tasks if it wasn't offered. My partner and I would review actual paid hours, mortgage costs and savings every three months, including the practice's confirmed plans rather than rumours. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep any paid physical work available and seek specific lender or family help only if our real budget showed a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but without the same rush as the two-year picture. I enjoy learning, and I can imagine using a decade well. I can't feed the children with ten years of possible progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count as progress at the first review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supervisor trusting me with one more task after checking my work, and the household reserve not shrinking. A better score on a trade-study app isn't the same as reliable paid work. I'd want to see the learning turn into reliable paid work before calling it security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a business to control your own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with this small a reserve and while I still need supervision in the trade. I'd need proper skill, the required permissions, real customers and money I could afford to lose. Liking risk doesn't make the money that keeps my children housed available to gamble.

say: I'd use **ten years** without spending money the household hasn't earned.
I'd plan the **children's next steps** without promising an unchanged working world.
think: I'll still need **earnings** around 53 and 56, without assumed retirement or mortgage clearance.
My **junior pay** and thin reserve still make a missed week worrying despite the longer warning.
do: Request the **funded course** with paid class hours now, keeping supervised work if refused.
Review **household hours** and mortgage costs quarterly using the practice's confirmed plans.
Keep **paid physical work** after 2036 and seek specific help only if actual income leaves a gap.
feel: **Anxious** about present household finances, with less urgency around distant automation and continued interest in learning.
S4.quote: A better score on a trade-study app isn't the same as reliable paid work.
fieldNote: The **longer warning** changes urgency rather than granting retirement, eliminating mortgage costs or converting a junior into a licensed independent contractor.
His **business refusal** is a concrete financial and skill limit: adaptive temperament does not erase children, low savings or required supervision.

steps.text: Take fault-finding course only with covered fees and paid class hours
Keep supervised work and review real household hours and mortgage costs quarterly
Seek specific agreed family or lender help if actual income falls short after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my partner's booking wage could be hit in 2028, then robots could reduce my junior work around 2031. Paid practical training, honest hours and a real conversation about the practice's plans would help. I'd want help that lets us keep earning rather than a sales pitch for a business we can't afford to start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether somebody curious about AI can also be frightened. I can be the first person to try a tool and still be the person counting school-shoe money at night. I want my children to see me learning, not pretending the numbers add up.

headlineQuote: I can be the first person to try a tool and still be the person counting school-shoe money at night.
portrait: Emeka is **43**, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, low pay and continuing supervision despite daily AI-assisted study.
His **partner books appointments**, and the household has two school-age children, a mortgage, three weeks saved and few nearby electrical employers.
He sees **two income clocks**: thinking AI threatens booking work first, with robots later reaching his physical junior tasks.
His **learning enthusiasm** remains bounded by employer-funded fees and paid class time, with no unaffordable business gamble or assumed retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens the partner's booking wage first, followed by possible junior-work losses when robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** and honest hours would support learning without losing household income.
A clear account of the **practice's plans** would help the couple prepare for the partner's booking exposure.
